title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.

I evaluated the reliability of ACS estimates for median owner-occupied home values across Colorado counties by calculating each estimate’s margin of error as a percentage of its reported value: (MOE/estimate)×100.Counties with a relative MOE below 5% were classified as high confidence, those between 5% and 10% as moderate confidence, and those above 10% as low confidence. These thresholds are interpretive rather than official Census reliability standards, but they create a useful distribution for this county-level analysis: 23 counties have high-confidence estimates, 20 have moderately reliable estimates, and 21 have low-confidence estimates.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
Colorado communities with the least reliable ACS estimates of median owner-occupied home values are primarily small, rural counties. Jackson County has the greatest uncertainty: its estimated median home value is $250,000, with a margin of error of ±$104,968, or 42.0% of the estimate. Other counties with relatively high uncertainty include San Miguel County (27.0%), San Juan County (23.1%), Kiowa County (20.6%), Bent County (19.2%), and Baca County (18.4%). Using the selected thresholds, nine counties fall into the low-confidence category, compared with 23 high-confidence and 32 moderate-reliability counties.
This pattern reflects how the American Community Survey (ACS) works. Unlike a complete census count, the ACS is a continuous sample survey. Its estimates are based on responses from a subset of households rather than every household. Smaller counties contain fewer households and therefore tend to produce smaller survey samples. Smaller samples create more sampling variability, which appears as a larger margin of error relative to the reported estimate. ACS sampling error is generally lower when the sample size is larger, while small-area estimates often require pooled multi-year data to achieve usable precision.
A state agency that allocates housing assistance, property-tax relief, or infrastructure funding based on median home values—but treats every county estimate as equally precise—could make poorly targeted decisions. Rural, low-population counties would be most vulnerable. For example, Jackson County could be classified as comparatively high-value or low-value based on an estimate with a confidence interval spanning roughly $145,032 to $354,968. Funding formulas that ignore this uncertainty could underfund communities with genuine housing need or direct funds away from them based on unstable measurements. Agencies should therefore incorporate MOEs, confidence intervals, or reliability flags when comparing counties and making resource-allocation decision.
Reflections
When assessing estimates of median owner-occupied home values, it is important to consider margins of error and confidence intervals, as these measures provide greater context for informed policy-making. Relying solely on arbitrary or point estimates may lead to misleading conclusions and ineffective policy decisions. Counties seeking to implement policies that produce meaningful change should therefore account for the uncertainty surrounding these estimates when evaluating housing conditions and allocating resources.

Propagate the margin of error. If you compute a derived value — a percentage, a ratio, a sum — its uncertainty depends on the uncertainty of its inputs, and you can’t just carry the original MOE along. The Census Bureau publishes formulas for this, and tidycensus implements them: moe_sum(), moe_prop(), moe_ratio(). Compute something derived, and get its margin of error right.

Decennial Census: every 10 years, full population count.
ACS (American Community Survey): sample-based (since 2005), gives detailed demographic/economic/housing data plus a margin of error (MOE) since it’s an estimate, not a full count.

1. YAML
YAML is the configuration block at the top of a .qmd file. It begins and ends with three dashes:
---
title: "My Portfolio"
author: "Emmanuel Sampson"
date: today
format: html
---
YAML can specify:

The title and author
The date
Output format, such as HTML
Table of contents settings
Whether code is shown or hidden
Other document-level options


Important YAML Rules

Indentation matters.
Use spaces, not tabs.
A colon must have a space after it:

title: "My Page"

YAML begins at the first line of the document.
The opening and closing --- lines must both be present.

A common error is incorrect indentation.
For example, this is wrong:
website:
navbar:
  title: "Portfolio"
Because navbar should be nested under website.
The correct version is:
website:
  navbar:
    title: "Portfolio"

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
This week focused on data visualization using ggplot2 and how uncertainty should be considered when working with American Community Survey (ACS) estimates.
The major topics were:

Anscombe’s Quartet and why visualization matters
The Grammar of Graphics
Building plots with ggplot2
Aesthetic mappings using aes()
Choosing the appropriate geom_*()
Margin of Error (MOE) and Standard Error (SE)
Coefficient of Variation (CV)
Derived uncertainty
Comparing ACS estimates over time
Confidence intervals for change

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
1. Anscombe’s Quartet: Why Visualization Matters
Reference was made to Anscombe’s Quartet, which demonstrates why we should visualize our data rather than relying only on summary statistics.
Anscombe’s Quartet consists of four datasets that have nearly identical statistical properties, including similar:

Means
Variances
Correlations
Regression lines

However, when the datasets are plotted, they look very different.
The important lesson is:

Datasets can have similar summary statistics but very different underlying patterns. Always visualize your data.

A mean, correlation coefficient, or regression line alone may hide:

Outliers
Nonlinear relationships
Clusters
Unusual observations
Different distributions

This is particularly important in urban spatial analysis because two neighborhoods, census tracts, counties, or cities may have similar summary statistics but very different underlying patterns.

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
2. Grammar of Graphics
The Grammar of Graphics is the conceptual foundation behind ggplot2.
A plot can be understood as a mapping from columns in our data to visual properties on a page or canvas.
For example:



Your Data
Visual Property




Estimate
Position on y-axis


Population
Position on x-axis


Reliability
Color


Margin of Error (MOE)
Size



In other words:
Data variable → Visual property
Suppose our census tract dataset contains:
tract | population | estimate | moe | reliability
We could map:

population → x-axis
estimate → y-axis
reliability → color
moe → size

This allows one visualization to communicate several dimensions of the data simultaneously.

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
3. How to Build a ggplot
A basic ggplot2 visualization consists of three important components:
#| eval: false
ggplot(data) +
  aes(...) +
  geom_*()
Think of this as:

Data — What dataset am I using?
Aesthetics — Which variables should control visual properties?
Geometry — What type of chart or graphical object should be drawn?



Step 1: Create the Canvas
#| eval: false
p <- ggplot(data)
ggplot(data) tells R which dataset we want to visualize.
At this stage, ggplot() creates essentially a blank canvas.
For example:
#| eval: false
ggplot(tract_data)



Step 2: Define Aesthetic Mappings
The aes() function defines the aesthetic mappings.
#| eval: false
aes(
  x = population,
  y = moe_pct
)
This tells ggplot2:

Put population on the x-axis.
Put moe_pct on the y-axis.

Aesthetics can include:

x
y
color
fill
size
shape
alpha

For example:
#| eval: false
aes(
  x = population,
  y = moe_pct,
  color = reliability
)
Here, reliability determines the color of each observation.



Step 3: Choose a Geometry
The geom_*() function determines the shape or type of chart.
For example:
#| eval: false
ggplot(tract_data) +
  aes(
    x = population,
    y = moe_pct
  ) +
  geom_point()
This produces a scatterplot.
Breaking it down:







Component
Purpose




ggplot(tract_data)
Selects the dataset


aes(x = population, y = moe_pct)
Maps variables to axes


geom_point()
Draws the observations as points

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
4. Inside aes() vs. Outside aes()
An important distinction in ggplot2 is whether a visual property is placed inside or outside aes().

Inside aes() = Map a Variable
Suppose the dataset contains a variable called reliability.
#| eval: false
ggplot(tract_data) +
  aes(
    x = population,
    y = moe_pct,
    color = reliability
  ) +
  geom_point()
Here:
#| eval: false
aes(color = reliability)
means:

Change the color of the points according to the values of the reliability variable.

The color therefore communicates information from the data.



Outside aes() = Set a Constant
Suppose we instead write:
#| eval: false
ggplot(tract_data) +
  aes(
    x = population,
    y = moe_pct
  ) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")
Now every point is blue.
"blue" is not a variable in the dataset. It is simply a decoration or constant visual property.


Rule to Remember

Inside aes() = map a variable.


Outside aes() = set a constant or decoration.

For example:
#| eval: false
aes(color = reliability)
means color represents the variable reliability.
Whereas:
#| eval: false
geom_point(color = "blue")
means make every point blue.
This distinction also applies to:

size
shape
fill
alpha

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
5. Choosing the Correct geom_*()
The geometry we use depends on the question we want the visualization to answer.



What do I want to know?
GEOM




How is a variable distributed?
geom_histogram()


How do two variables relate?
geom_point()


How do groups compare?
geom_boxplot()


How do things change over time?
geom_line()


How uncertain is a value?
geom_errorbar()





How Is a Variable Distributed?
Use:
#| eval: false
geom_histogram()
Example:
#| eval: false
ggplot(county_data) +
  aes(x = estimate) +
  geom_histogram()
A histogram can help identify:

The center of a distribution
Spread
Skewness
Outliers
Multiple peaks




How Do Two Variables Relate?
Use:
#| eval: false
geom_point()
Example:
#| eval: false
ggplot(county_data) +
  aes(
    x = population,
    y = estimate
  ) +
  geom_point()
This produces a scatterplot that can help us examine whether two variables appear to be related.



How Do Groups Compare?
Use:
#| eval: false
geom_boxplot()
Example:
#| eval: false
ggplot(county_data) +
  aes(
    x = reliability,
    y = estimate
  ) +
  geom_boxplot()
Boxplots are useful for comparing distributions between different groups.



How Do Things Change Over Time?
Use:
#| eval: false
geom_line()
Example:
#| eval: false
ggplot(data) +
  aes(
    x = year,
    y = estimate
  ) +
  geom_line()
Line charts are particularly useful for showing change over time.



How Uncertain Is a Value?
Use:
#| eval: false
geom_errorbar()
For example:
#| eval: false
ggplot(county_data) +
  aes(
    x = county,
    y = estimate,
    ymin = estimate - moe,
    ymax = estimate + moe
  ) +
  geom_errorbar()
Error bars allow us to visualize the uncertainty surrounding an estimate.

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
6. ACS Estimates and Uncertainty
The American Community Survey (ACS) is based on a sample of the population.
Therefore, ACS values are estimates, not exact measurements.
Each estimate comes with uncertainty.
For example:
\[
\$45,000 \pm \$8,000
\]
Here:

$45,000 is the estimate.
$8,000 is the Margin of Error (MOE).

The MOE tells us about the uncertainty surrounding the estimate.
ACS published margins of error generally correspond to a 90% confidence level.
This is important when using ACS data for urban policy analysis because an estimate should not be interpreted without considering its uncertainty.

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
section: 7. Margin of Error and Standard Error
text:
7. Margin of Error and Standard Error
For a 90% confidence interval:
\[
MOE = 1.645 \times SE
\]
Therefore:
\[
SE = \frac{MOE}{1.645}
\]
where:

MOE = Margin of Error
SE = Standard Error
1.645 = critical value associated with a 90% confidence interval


Example
Suppose:
\[
Estimate = \$45,000
\]
and:
\[
MOE = \$8,000
\]
Then:
\[
SE = \frac{8,000}{1.645}
\]
Therefore:
\[
SE \approx \$4,863
\]
The standard error provides a measure of the sampling variability associated with the estimate.

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
8. Coefficient of Variation (CV)
The Coefficient of Variation (CV) is a relative measure of sampling error.
It measures uncertainty relative to the size of the estimate.
The formula is:
\[
CV = \frac{SE}{Estimate} \times 100
\]
Since:
\[
SE = \frac{MOE}{1.645}
\]
we can also calculate CV as:
\[
CV = \frac{MOE/1.645}{Estimate} \times 100
\]

Reliability Classification
The classification discussed in class was:







Coefficient of Variation
Interpretation




CV < 15%
Low sampling error / high reliability


CV = 15%–30%
Medium sampling error / moderate reliability


CV > 30%
High sampling error / lower reliability



The general relationship is:

Lower CV → greater relative precision


Higher CV → greater relative sampling uncertainty

These thresholds are useful for classifying estimates, but they should be understood as practical thresholds rather than universal statistical laws.

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
9. Example of Coefficient of Variation
Consider two census tracts.

Tract A
Suppose:
\[
Estimate = \$100,000
\]
and:
\[
SE = \$5,000
\]
Then:
\[
CV = \frac{5,000}{100,000} \times 100
\]
\[
CV = 5\%
\]
This represents relatively low sampling error.


Tract B
Suppose:
\[
Estimate = \$10,000
\]
and:
\[
SE = \$5,000
\]
Then:
\[
CV = \frac{5,000}{10,000} \times 100
\]
\[
CV = 50\%
\]
Both estimates have the same standard error of $5,000, but the uncertainty is much larger relative to the estimate for Tract B.
This demonstrates why CV is useful.

Absolute uncertainty alone does not tell the whole story. The CV evaluates uncertainty relative to the size of the estimate.

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
10. Derived Uncertainty
Sometimes we use ACS estimates to calculate a new statistic.
For example:
\[
Poverty\ Rate =
\frac{Number\ of\ People\ in\ Poverty}
{Total\ Population}
\]
Both the numerator and denominator have their own margins of error.
Conceptually:
\[
Poverty\ Rate =
\frac{Population\ in\ Poverty \pm MOE}
{Total\ Population \pm MOE}
\]
We cannot simply calculate the poverty rate and ignore the uncertainty associated with the original estimates.
Instead, we must propagate the uncertainty from the original variables into the new statistic.
This is known as derived uncertainty.

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
section: 11. Functions for Derived Margins of Error
text:
11. Functions for Derived Margins of Error
Different calculations require different approaches to uncertainty.

moe_sum()
Use moe_sum() when adding estimates together.
Conceptually:
#| eval: false
moe_sum(...)
For example, several age categories might be combined to calculate a larger population group.
Importantly, we generally do not simply add the margins of error together.



moe_prop()
Use moe_prop() when one estimate is expressed as a proportion of another and the numerator is a subset of the denominator.
For example:
\[
Poverty\ Rate =
\frac{Population\ in\ Poverty}
{Total\ Population}
\]
The population in poverty is part of the total population.
Therefore, this is a proportion.
Conceptually:
#| eval: false
moe_prop(...)



moe_ratio()
Use moe_ratio() when calculating a ratio where the numerator is not a subset of the denominator.
Conceptually:
#| eval: false
moe_ratio(...)


Important Difference

Proportion: The numerator is contained within the denominator.


Ratio: The numerator is not contained within the denominator.

This distinction matters because the uncertainty calculations are different.

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
section: 12. Change Over Time with ACS Data
text:
12. Change Over Time with ACS Data
Comparing ACS estimates over time requires special care.
One important issue is overlapping five-year estimates.
Consider:

2018–2022 ACS 5-year estimate
2019–2023 ACS 5-year estimate

These two periods overlap substantially.
They both contain data from:

2019
2020
2021
2022

Therefore, they are not independent five-year periods.
For a cleaner comparison, use non-overlapping periods.
For example:
2014–2018 vs. 2019–2023
There are no overlapping years between these two periods.

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
13. Example: Measuring Change Over Time
Suppose we have the following ACS estimates.

2014–2018
\[
\$45,000 \pm \$8,000
\]


2019–2023
\[
\$62,000 \pm \$11,000
\]
The difference between the point estimates is:
\[
\$62,000 - \$45,000 = \$17,000
\]
At first glance, we might conclude that the value increased by $17,000.
However, both estimates contain uncertainty.
We therefore need to determine the uncertainty associated with the difference between the two estimates.

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
14. Standard Error of the Difference
First, convert each MOE into a standard error.

First Period
\[
SE_1 = \frac{8,000}{1.645}
\]
\[
SE_1 \approx 4,863
\]


Second Period
\[
SE_2 = \frac{11,000}{1.645}
\]
\[
SE_2 \approx 6,687
\]
For independent estimates, the standard error of the difference is:
\[
SE_{diff} =
\sqrt{SE_1^2 + SE_2^2}
\]
Therefore:
\[
SE_{diff} =
\sqrt{4,863^2 + 6,687^2}
\]
\[
SE_{diff} \approx 8,268
\]
Notice that we did not calculate:
\[
8,000 + 11,000
\]
We do not simply add the margins of error.

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
15. Confidence Interval for the Change
Our estimated change is:
\[
\$17,000
\]
and:
\[
SE_{diff} \approx \$8,268
\]
For a 90% confidence interval:
\[
Difference \pm (1.645 \times SE_{diff})
\]
Therefore:
\[
17,000 \pm (1.645 \times 8,268)
\]
\[
17,000 \pm 13,601
\]
The approximate confidence interval is therefore:
\[
[\$3,399,\ \$30,601]
\]
The entire interval is above zero.
Under the assumptions of this calculation, this provides evidence that the observed increase is statistically distinguishable from zero at the 90% confidence level.

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
16. Why Zero Matters
Suppose instead that the confidence interval for a change was:
\[
[-\$4,000,\ \$20,000]
\]
This interval contains:
\[
0
\]
That means the data are compatible with:

A decrease
Essentially no change
An increase

We therefore would not conclude that the estimated change is statistically distinguishable from zero at that confidence level.
The important lesson is:

A difference between two point estimates does not automatically mean that there has been a statistically distinguishable change.

We must consider the uncertainty surrounding both estimates.

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
17. Visualizing Reliability
The concepts of visualization and uncertainty can be combined in ggplot2.
For example:
#| eval: false
ggplot(tract_data) +
  aes(
    x = population,
    y = estimate,
    color = reliability
  ) +
  geom_point()
This visualization communicates three pieces of information:



Variable
Visual Property




Population
x-axis


Estimate
y-axis


Reliability
Color



This allows us to see not only the estimates themselves but also how reliable those estimates are.

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
18. Visualizing Margins of Error
We can also display uncertainty directly using error bars.
#| eval: false
ggplot(county_data) +
  aes(
    x = county,
    y = estimate,
    ymin = estimate - moe,
    ymax = estimate + moe
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar()
The point represents the estimate.
The error bar represents the uncertainty around that estimate.
This is particularly important when comparing ACS estimates because two point estimates may look different while still having substantial uncertainty around them.

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
19. Connecting the Main Ideas
The topics from this week are closely connected.

Visualization
Anscombe’s Quartet teaches us:

Do not rely only on summary statistics. Visualize the data.



Grammar of Graphics
A visualization maps:
\[
Data \rightarrow Visual\ Properties
\]
In ggplot2, the basic structure is:
#| eval: false
ggplot(data) +
  aes(...) +
  geom_*()


Aesthetic Mapping
Remember:
#| eval: false
aes(color = reliability)
means:
Map the variable reliability to color.
While:
#| eval: false
geom_point(color = "blue")
means:
Make every point blue.


ACS Uncertainty
For ACS data:
\[
SE = \frac{MOE}{1.645}
\]
The Coefficient of Variation is:
\[
CV = \frac{SE}{Estimate} \times 100
\]
For two independent estimates:
\[
SE_{diff} =
\sqrt{SE_1^2 + SE_2^2}
\]
The 90% confidence interval for the difference is:
\[
Difference \pm 1.645(SE_{diff})
\]

title: Week 2: Data Visualization and Uncertainty
text:
20. Key Concepts to Remember

Anscombe’s Quartet demonstrates why data should be visualized rather than understood only through summary statistics.
The Grammar of Graphics treats a plot as a mapping between variables and visual properties.
ggplot(data) identifies the dataset and creates the canvas.
aes() defines aesthetic mappings.
geom_*() determines the type of graphical object.
Inside aes() means map a variable.
Outside aes() means set a constant visual property.
geom_histogram() shows the distribution of a variable.
geom_point() shows relationships between variables.
geom_boxplot() compares groups.
geom_line() shows change over time.
geom_errorbar() visualizes uncertainty.
ACS data are estimates, so uncertainty must be considered.
ACS margins of error generally correspond to a 90% confidence level.
Standard Error can be calculated as MOE / 1.645.
The Coefficient of Variation measures uncertainty relative to the size of an estimate.
A high CV indicates relatively high sampling uncertainty.
Derived statistics require the uncertainty of the original estimates to be propagated.
moe_sum() is used when combining estimates.
moe_prop() is appropriate for proportions where the numerator is a subset of the denominator.
moe_ratio() is appropriate for ratios where the numerator is not a subset of the denominator.
Be careful when comparing overlapping ACS 5-year periods.
For straightforward change comparisons, non-overlapping periods are preferable.
A difference between two estimates does not automatically mean the change is statistically distinguishable from zero.
When the confidence interval for a difference includes zero, the evidence does not distinguish the estimated change from zero at that confidence level.

text:
How did poverty change across Philadelphia, and how much confidence can we place in those changes? This analysis compares estimates from the American Community Survey (ACS) for 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. It examines census tracts, small statistical areas that help describe conditions within the city. Each estimate represents a five-year period.

title: Assignment 3: Measuring Poverty in Philadelphia
section: Poverty rates and margins of error
text:
Poverty rates and margins of error
The ACS surveys a sample of residents, so its estimates carry sampling uncertainty. A margin of error (MOE) describes that uncertainty: a larger MOE means a less precise estimate. A poverty rate of 25% with an MOE of 5 percentage points gives an approximate 90% confidence interval of 20%–30%. Across repeated samples, intervals calculated this way would contain the true value about 90% of the time.
The calculations account for uncertainty in both the number of people below the poverty level and the population used to calculate the rate, using the proportion method documented by tidycensus.


Show code
calculate_rates <- function(data, period_label) {
  data %>%
    mutate(
      # Treat unavailable values and Census missing-data codes as missing.
      across(c(total_popE, total_popM, povertyE, povertyM),
             ~ replace(.x, !is.finite(.x) | .x < 0, NA_real_)),
      denominator = if_else(total_popE > 0 & !is.na(povertyE) &
                              povertyE <= total_popE, total_popE, NA_real_),
      poverty_rate = 100 * povertyE / denominator,
      poverty_rate_moe = 100 * moe_prop(
        povertyE, denominator, povertyM, total_popM
      ),
      lower_90 = pmax(0, poverty_rate - poverty_rate_moe),
      upper_90 = pmin(100, poverty_rate + poverty_rate_moe),
      period = period_label
    ) %>% select(-denominator)
}
poverty_2010 <- calculate_rates(poverty_2010, "2006-2010")
poverty_2017 <- calculate_rates(poverty_2017, "2013-2017")

text:
Reliability of tract estimates
To compare precision across tracts, this analysis expresses each margin of error as a percentage of its estimated poverty rate. This relative MOE is smaller when the estimate is more precise. For example, an MOE of 5 percentage points around a rate of 25% gives a relative MOE of 20%.
This analysis labels relative MOEs below 12% as reliable, 12% to less than 40% as somewhat reliable, and 40% or above as unreliable. These thresholds are specific to this analysis. A relative margin of error cannot be calculated when the estimated poverty rate is zero, because that would require dividing by zero. These cases and missing data are listed separately.


Show code
classify_reliability <- function(data) {
  data %>% mutate(
    moe_pct = 100 * poverty_rate_moe /
      if_else(poverty_rate > 0, poverty_rate, NA_real_),
    reliability = case_when(
      is.na(poverty_rate) | is.na(poverty_rate_moe) ~ "No valid estimate/MOE",
      poverty_rate == 0 ~ "Zero estimate: relative MOE undefined",
      moe_pct < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      moe_pct < 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )
}
poverty_2010 <- classify_reliability(poverty_2010) %>% st_transform(4326)
poverty_2017 <- classify_reliability(poverty_2017) %>% st_transform(4326)
poverty_change <- bind_rows(poverty_2010, poverty_2017)

reliability_summary <- poverty_change %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(period, reliability, name = "tracts") %>%
  group_by(period) %>% mutate(percent = 100 * tracts / sum(tracts)) %>%
  ungroup()

  st_drop_geometry(poverty_2010) %>% transmute(GEOID, in_2010 = TRUE),

  select(GEOID, period, poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = GEOID, names_from = period,

The change is the later poverty rate minus the earlier rate. For example, an increase from 20% to 25% is a rise of 5 percentage points. Assuming independent estimates for these non-overlapping periods, the change MOE is the square root of the sum of the squared MOEs. A change is significant at approximately the 90% level when its absolute value exceeds this MOE. Each tract is tested separately, without adjusting for the number of tests. With many tests, some changes may appear significant by chance. Failure to detect a change does not prove poverty stayed constant.

)

Plot of change and its uncertainty
In the formulas below, \(p\) is the poverty rate, \(\Delta\) is the change between periods, and \(MOE\) is the margin of error. Rates and changes are expressed in percentage points for these calculations.
\[
\Delta = p_{2013-2017} - p_{2006-2010}, \qquad
MOE_{\Delta} = \sqrt{MOE_{2013-2017}^{2} + MOE_{2006-2010}^{2}}.
\]
The graph shows every tract for which a change can be calculated, ordered from the largest decrease to the largest increase. Each point is an estimated change; each vertical line spans \(\Delta \pm MOE_{\Delta}\). Both are in percentage points. A confidence interval entirely above or below the dashed zero line indicates a statistically significant change at 90% confidence. Intervals that touch or cross zero do not establish a change at this confidence level. The intervals use a normal approximation and are shown in full. For a few tracts, large margins of error extend beyond the possible range of -100 to 100 percentage points. These wide intervals show how uncertain the estimates are; changes beyond that range are not physically possible.

  geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Significant decrease" = "#0072B2",
               "No significant change" = "#777777",
               "Significant increase" = "#D55E00"),
    breaks = c("Significant decrease", "No significant change",
               "Significant increase"),
    drop = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Change in poverty rates across Philadelphia census tracts",
    subtitle = "2013-2017 minus 2006-2010; intervals show uncertainty in the change",
    x = "Tracts ordered by estimated change",
    y = "Change in poverty rate (percentage points)",
    color = NULL,
    caption = paste(nrow(change_plot_data), "tracts shown;",
                    nrow(poverty_wide) - nrow(change_plot_data),
                    "tracts omitted because change cannot be estimated.")
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0))








Figure 1: Philadelphia tract poverty-rate changes, 2006–2010 to 2013–2017. Points show estimated changes; vertical lines show 90% confidence intervals for those changes. Tracts are ordered by estimated change, not geographic location.





Results. Of 384 census tracts across the two periods, 36 show a significant increase and 27 show a significant decrease at the 90% level. There are 313 tracts with no statistically detectable change and 8 without sufficient data. These counts describe how many areas experienced detectable changes. Because tracts have different populations, the counts alone do not show whether Philadelphia’s overall poverty rate increased or decreased.

text:
7. Geometry Is “Sticky” in sf
In R, spatial data are commonly handled using the sf package.
sf stands for:

Simple Features

An sf object behaves much like a normal data frame, except that it contains a special geometry column.
One important characteristic is that:

Geometry is sticky.

This means many data manipulation operations preserve the geometry column automatically.
For example:
#| eval: false
tracts %>%
  select(GEOID, med_income)
If tracts is an sf object, the resulting object will generally still retain its geometry.
This is useful because we can use familiar dplyr operations while keeping the spatial information attached.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
8. Common Spatial Data Formats
Spatial data can be stored in several formats.
Common examples include:

Shapefile
.shp
A shapefile is a traditional vector spatial data format.
A shapefile is actually made up of several associated files, commonly including:
.shp
.shx
.dbf
.prj
These files work together to store:

Geometry
Attributes
Coordinate system information




File Geodatabase
.gdb
A geodatabase can contain multiple spatial datasets and tables.
It is commonly associated with the ArcGIS ecosystem.



Simple Features (sf)
In R, spatial vector data are commonly represented as sf objects.
For example:
#| eval: false
library(sf)

tracts <- st_read("tracts.shp")

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
9. Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)
A Coordinate Reference System (CRS) tells us how coordinates correspond to locations on Earth.
Without a CRS, numbers such as:
-75.16, 39.95
or
2,700,000, 240,000
do not tell us enough about where a location actually is.
The CRS provides the framework for interpreting those coordinates.
There are two major categories discussed in class:







Geographic CRS
Projected CRS




Coordinates commonly expressed in angular units such as degrees
Coordinates expressed in linear units


Represents locations relative to an Earth model
Represents locations on a flat map


Longitude and latitude are common
Easting and northing are common


Useful for global location/reference
Often useful for local or regional analysis


Units commonly degrees
Units commonly meters or feet

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
10. Geographic Coordinate Systems
A geographic coordinate system represents locations using angular coordinates.
The two most familiar coordinates are:

Latitude
Longitude

Latitude measures position north or south of the Equator.
Longitude measures position east or west of a reference meridian, conventionally the Prime Meridian through Greenwich.
For example:
Longitude = -75.16°
Latitude = 39.95°
approximately identifies a location in Philadelphia.
Because these are angular measurements, the units are degrees, not meters or feet.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
11. The Equator
The Equator is an imaginary line around the Earth located at:
\[
0^\circ \text{ latitude}
\]
Latitude is measured north or south from the Equator.
Values range approximately from:
\[
90^\circ S
\]
to:
\[
90^\circ N
\]
Therefore:

The Equator provides the zero reference for latitude.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
12. The Greenwich Meridian
The Prime Meridian, conventionally passing through Greenwich, England, is defined as:
\[
0^\circ \text{ longitude}
\]
Longitude is measured east or west from this reference.
Therefore:

The Equator is the reference for latitude, while the Prime Meridian is the reference for longitude.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
section: 13. Why We Need an Earth Model
text:
13. Why We Need an Earth Model
The Earth is not a perfect sphere.
It is slightly flattened near the poles and wider around the Equator.
To represent the Earth mathematically, geodesy uses simplified models.
Important terms include:

Ellipsoid
Geoid
Flattening ratio
Datum

These concepts help connect locations on the real Earth to coordinate systems.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
14. Ellipsoid
An ellipsoid is a smooth mathematical approximation of the Earth’s shape.
Instead of modeling every mountain, valley, and variation in gravity, an ellipsoid provides a simplified mathematical surface.
Important properties include:

Semi-major axis
Semi-minor axis
Flattening

The Earth is commonly modeled as an oblate ellipsoid because it is slightly wider around the Equator than from pole to pole.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
15. Flattening Ratio
The flattening of an ellipsoid describes how much the ellipsoid differs from a perfect sphere.
Conceptually:
\[
f = \frac{a-b}{a}
\]
where:

(a) = semi-major axis
(b) = semi-minor axis
(f) = flattening

If:
\[
a=b
\]
the object would be a perfect sphere.
Because the Earth is slightly flattened at the poles:
\[
a>b
\]

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
16. The Geoid
The geoid is a model of the Earth’s gravity-based shape.
It can be thought of approximately as the surface that the oceans would follow under the influence of gravity if other forces such as tides and currents were removed and the surface extended through the continents.
Unlike a smooth mathematical ellipsoid, the geoid is irregular because Earth’s gravity varies spatially.
A useful distinction is:

Ellipsoid = simplified mathematical Earth


Geoid = gravity-based representation of Earth’s shape

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
17. Datums
A geodetic datum provides the reference framework used to connect coordinates to the Earth.
A datum typically incorporates an Earth model and defines how that model is positioned or realized relative to the Earth.
Important examples include:

NAD27
NAD83
WGS84

Changing the datum can change the coordinates assigned to the same real-world location.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
18. Clarke 1866 and NAD27
The Clarke 1866 ellipsoid was historically used because it provided a useful approximation of the Earth’s shape for North America.
The North American Datum of 1927 (NAD27) used the Clarke 1866 ellipsoid and was anchored to a reference location at Meades Ranch, Kansas.
Conceptually:
Clarke 1866 ellipsoid
        +
Meades Ranch reference
        ↓
NAD27
NAD27 is an older datum and has largely been replaced by more modern systems.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
19. NAD83 and GRS80
The North American Datum of 1983 (NAD83) replaced NAD27 for much modern mapping in North America.
NAD83 is closely associated with the GRS80 ellipsoid.
GRS80 means:

Geodetic Reference System 1980

Compared with NAD27, NAD83 was developed using improved geodetic measurements and a geocentric approach.
Therefore:
NAD27 → Clarke 1866
NAD83 → GRS80
is a useful association to remember.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
20. WGS84
WGS84 stands for:

World Geodetic System 1984

It is the reference system widely associated with the Global Positioning System (GPS).
A common geographic CRS based on WGS84 is:
EPSG:4326
Its coordinates are commonly represented as longitude and latitude.
For example:
Longitude: -75.16
Latitude:   39.95
A useful association is:

WGS84 → GPS

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
21. Geographic vs. Projected Coordinate Systems
A major distinction in spatial analysis is between geographic and projected coordinate systems.

Geographic
A geographic CRS commonly uses:
longitude
latitude
with angular units such as:
degrees


Projected
A projected CRS transforms locations onto a flat coordinate system.
Coordinates are typically expressed as:
Easting
Northing
with linear units such as:
meters
feet
The main idea is:

When working in a projected coordinate system, we can often work directly with meaningful linear units such as feet or meters rather than angular degrees.

This can be especially useful for local spatial analysis involving distance, area, and buffers.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
22. The Projection Problem
The Earth is curved.
A map is flat.
Therefore, converting the Earth’s curved surface into a flat map necessarily introduces some form of distortion.
A projection may distort one or more of the following:

Shape
Area
Distance
Direction

A useful memory device from class is:

SADD

S = Shape
A = Area
D = Distance
D = Direction
No flat map projection can preserve all of these properties perfectly everywhere.
Therefore:

The appropriate projection depends on what we need to preserve for our analysis.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
23. Conformal Projections
A conformal projection is designed to preserve local angles and shapes.
It is useful when maintaining local shape is particularly important.
However, preserving shape comes at the cost of distortion in other properties, especially area over larger regions.
The Mercator projection is a well-known example of a conformal projection.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
24. Equal-Area Projections
An equal-area projection preserves area.
This means that areas shown on the map maintain their correct proportional relationship.
This can be particularly important when mapping phenomena where the size of geographic areas matters.
For example:
Albers Equal Area
is a commonly used equal-area projection.

Equal-area → preserve area

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
25. Equidistant Projections
An equidistant projection preserves certain distances from specified points or along specified lines.
It does not mean that every possible distance everywhere on the map is perfectly preserved.

Equidistant → preserves particular distances under the design of the projection

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
26. Projection Surfaces
Projection concepts are often described using geometric surfaces.
Common families include:

Cylindrical
Conceptually, the globe is projected onto a cylinder.


Conic
Conceptually, the globe is projected onto a cone.
Conic projections are often useful for regions extending predominantly east-west in the mid-latitudes.


Planar / Azimuthal
Conceptually, the globe is projected onto a plane.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
27. Line of Tangency
A line of tangency is where a projection surface touches the globe or reference surface.
Distortion is generally lowest along or near the contact between the projection surface and the reference surface.
For example, a cone may touch the globe along a particular latitude.
That line of contact is related to where the projection provides particularly good geometric correspondence.
Some projection systems instead use secant surfaces that intersect the globe along two lines.
The broader principle is:

Distortion generally increases as we move away from the projection’s areas of optimal contact.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
28. Transverse Cylindrical Projections
A standard cylindrical projection can be imagined as wrapping a cylinder around the Earth.
In a transverse cylindrical projection, the cylinder is conceptually rotated so that its orientation is better suited to regions extending north-south.
The Transverse Mercator projection is extremely important in modern GIS.
It forms the basis of the UTM system.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
29. Examples of Coordinate Systems







CRS / Projection
Typical Units




Pennsylvania State Plane
US survey feet or meters depending on CRS definition


Albers Equal Area
Commonly meters


WGS84 geographic CRS
Degrees


NAD83 geographic CRS
Degrees



The exact units should always be checked from the CRS rather than assumed from its name.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
30. State Plane Coordinate Systems
The State Plane Coordinate System was designed to provide relatively accurate mapping within smaller regions of the United States.
States may be divided into multiple zones to minimize distortion.
For example, Pennsylvania has State Plane zones including:
Pennsylvania North
Pennsylvania South
A commonly encountered Pennsylvania South State Plane CRS is:
EPSG:2272
which uses US survey feet.
State Plane systems are particularly useful for local and regional work where accurate linear measurements are important.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
31. Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM)
The Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) system divides most of the world into zones.
UTM has:

60 zones

Each zone is:

6 degrees of longitude wide

This is an important correction:
6 degrees
not:
6 meters
Each zone uses its own Transverse Mercator projection.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
32. UTM Coordinates
UTM coordinates are expressed primarily as:

Easting
Northing

and the units are:
meters
A false easting is used so that the central meridian of each UTM zone is assigned an easting of:
\[
500,000 \text{ meters}
\]
This helps avoid negative easting values within a normal UTM zone.
Because each UTM zone has its own coordinate system, the same numerical coordinate values can occur in different zones.
Therefore, a UTM coordinate is incomplete unless we also know information such as:

UTM zone
Hemisphere
Datum / CRS

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
33. EPSG Codes
CRSs are often identified using EPSG codes.
For example:
EPSG:4326
is commonly used for WGS84 longitude/latitude.
Another example relevant to Philadelphia is:
EPSG:2272
which corresponds to a Pennsylvania South State Plane CRS using US survey feet.
EPSG codes make it much easier to specify exactly which coordinate reference system we are using.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
34. Checking a CRS with st_crs()
Before conducting spatial analysis, it is good practice to check the CRS.
#| eval: false
st_crs(data)
This can tell us information such as:

CRS name
EPSG code
Datum
Projection
Coordinate units

This is particularly important because spatial functions such as buffers and distances depend on the coordinate system and its units.

Good Practice

Check the CRS before performing spatial analysis.

#| eval: false
st_crs(data)

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
35. st_set_crs() — Assigning a CRS
st_set_crs() assigns CRS information to spatial data.
Conceptually, it says:

These existing coordinate values should be interpreted using this CRS.

For example:
#| eval: false
data <- st_set_crs(data, 2272)
This does not mathematically transform the coordinates.
It changes or assigns the CRS metadata.

Important

st_set_crs() changes the CRS label, not the underlying coordinate values.

Use it when the coordinates are already in a known CRS but that CRS information is missing or incorrect.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
36. st_transform() — Transforming Coordinates
st_transform() is different.
It mathematically transforms the coordinates from one CRS to another.
For example:
#| eval: false
data_wgs84 <- st_transform(data, 4326)
If data is currently in EPSG:2272, this converts the coordinates into EPSG:4326.
The actual coordinate values change.
For example, projected coordinates might look conceptually like:
2,700,000
240,000
After transformation to WGS84, they might look like:
-75.16
39.95
Therefore:

st_set_crs() assigns or corrects the CRS label.


st_transform() actually changes the coordinate representation.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
37. st_set_crs() vs. st_transform()
This distinction is extremely important.



Function
What does it do?
Coordinates change?




st_crs()
Checks CRS information
No


st_set_crs()
Assigns/replaces CRS metadata
No


st_transform()
Converts coordinates to another CRS
Yes



A useful workflow is:
#| eval: false

# Check CRS
st_crs(data)

# Transform if necessary
data_projected <- st_transform(data, 2272)

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
38. Buffers
A buffer creates an area around a spatial feature.
For example:
#| eval: false
station_buffer <- st_buffer(stations, 500)
This creates a buffer around each station.
But what does 500 mean?
That depends on the CRS and how sf interprets its units.
For projected data, it generally corresponds to the linear units associated with the CRS.
Therefore, before creating a buffer:
#| eval: false
st_crs(stations)
Check the CRS and units.

Important Principle

Never interpret a buffer distance without knowing the CRS and units.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
39. Example: Half-Mile Station Buffer
Suppose our data use a State Plane CRS measured in feet.
Half a mile is:
\[
0.5 \times 5,280 = 2,640 \text{ feet}
\]
We could therefore create:
#| eval: false
station_buffer <- st_buffer(
  stations,
  dist = 2640
)
This represents a half-mile buffer if the CRS uses feet.
This demonstrates why checking:
#| eval: false
st_crs(stations)
is essential.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
40. Spatial Relationships
Spatial analysis often asks whether two geographic objects have a particular relationship.
For example:

Do they intersect?
Do they touch?
Is one within another?
How far apart are they?

Suppose we have geographic objects:
A
B
C
Different spatial predicates answer different questions about their relationships.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
41. st_intersects()
st_intersects() asks whether two geometries share any spatial location.
Conceptually:
#| eval: false
st_intersects(A, B)
If A and B overlap or touch, they intersect.
An object also intersects itself.
Conceptually:



Relationship
st_intersects()




A with B
TRUE if they share any point


A with C
TRUE if they share any point


A with A
TRUE



The key idea is:

Intersect means the geometries have at least one point in common.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
42. st_touches()
st_touches() asks whether two geometries share a boundary but their interiors do not overlap.
For example, two neighboring census tracts may share a border.
They:
touch = TRUE
but one is not inside the other.
Conceptually:
#| eval: false
st_touches(A, B)
This is particularly useful for identifying neighboring polygons.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
43. st_within()
st_within() asks whether one geometry lies completely inside another geometry.
For example:
Station → Census tract
If a station point lies inside a census tract polygon:
#| eval: false
st_within(station, tract)
would return a spatial relationship indicating that the station is within that tract.
The order matters.

st_within(A, B) asks whether A is within B.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
44. Comparing Spatial Predicates
A simplified conceptual comparison is:







Function
Question




st_intersects(A, B)
Do A and B share any spatial location?


st_touches(A, B)
Do their boundaries touch without interior overlap?


st_within(A, B)
Is A inside B?



These relationships are not interchangeable.
The correct function depends on the spatial question being asked.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
45. st_filter()
st_filter() filters one spatial dataset based on its spatial relationship with another.
For example:
#| eval: false
nearby_tracts <- st_filter(
  tracts,
  station_buffer
)
This can be used to identify tracts that spatially interact with the station buffer.
A question such as:

How many census tracts are within or intersect a half-mile station area?

could begin with a buffer followed by a spatial filter.
#| eval: false
station_buffer <- st_buffer(stations, 2640)

nearby_tracts <- st_filter(
  tracts,
  station_buffer
)

nrow(nearby_tracts)
assuming the data are projected in feet.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
46. st_intersection()
st_intersection() actually creates the geometry representing the overlap between spatial objects.
For example:
#| eval: false
tract_station_overlap <- st_intersection(
  tracts,
  station_buffer
)
Unlike a simple predicate, this can change the geometry.
A census tract may be clipped to only the portion falling inside a station buffer.
Therefore:

st_intersects() asks whether an intersection exists.


st_intersection() creates the overlapping geometry.

This distinction is important.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
47. st_union()
st_union() combines spatial geometries.
For example:
#| eval: false
combined_buffer <- st_union(station_buffer)
If several station buffers overlap, st_union() can dissolve them into a combined geometry.
Conceptually:
Multiple geometries
        ↓
    st_union()
        ↓
Combined geometry
This can be useful when we care about the overall service area rather than the individual station buffers.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
text:
49. A Typical Spatial Analysis Workflow
Suppose the research question is:

How many census tracts are near a transit station?


Step 1: Check the CRS
#| eval: false
st_crs(stations)
st_crs(tracts)


Step 2: Make sure both layers use an appropriate common CRS
#| eval: false
stations <- st_transform(stations, 2272)
tracts <- st_transform(tracts, 2272)


Step 3: Create the station buffer
If the units are feet and we want half a mile:
#| eval: false
station_buffer <- st_buffer(
  stations,
  dist = 2640
)


Step 4: Find intersecting tracts
#| eval: false
nearby_tracts <- st_filter(
  tracts,
  station_buffer
)


Step 5: Count the tracts
#| eval: false
nrow(nearby_tracts)
This demonstrates how CRS, buffers, spatial relationships, and filtering work together in a real spatial analysis.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Coordinate Reference Systems, and Spatial Operations
section: 50. Key Distinction: Attribute Joins vs. Spatial Joins
text:
50. Key Distinction: Attribute Joins vs. Spatial Joins
There are two important ways of connecting datasets.

Attribute Join
An attribute join uses a common variable such as:
GEOID
Example:
#| eval: false
left_join(
  tracts,
  income,
  by = "GEOID"
)
The relationship is determined by matching values.


Spatial Join / Spatial Filter
A spatial operation uses the geographic relationship between geometries.
For example:
#| eval: false
st_filter(
  tracts,
  station_buffer
)
The relationship is determined by location rather than a common ID.


Important Difference

Attribute join → “Do these records have the same key?”


Spatial relationship → “Do these geographic objects occupy related locations?”

52. Key Concepts to Remember

A GEOID can be used as the key for joining Census and ACS datasets.
left_join() keeps all observations from the left dataset.
inner_join() keeps only observations appearing in both datasets.
full_join() keeps observations from both datasets.
sf stands for Simple Features.
An sf object contains normal attributes plus a geometry column.
Geometry is described as sticky because it is generally retained during many dplyr operations.
A CRS tells us how coordinates correspond to locations on Earth.
Geographic CRSs commonly use longitude and latitude expressed in degrees.
Projected CRSs use planar coordinates commonly expressed in meters or feet.
The Earth is not a perfect sphere.
An ellipsoid is a smooth mathematical approximation of Earth’s shape.
The geoid represents a gravity-based model of Earth’s shape.
NAD27 is associated with the Clarke 1866 ellipsoid and the historical Meades Ranch reference.
NAD83 is closely associated with GRS80.
WGS84 is the reference system associated with GPS.
EPSG:4326 is commonly used for WGS84 longitude/latitude.
Every flat map projection introduces distortion.
Remember SADD: Shape, Area, Distance, Direction.
Conformal projections preserve local angles and shapes.
Equal-area projections preserve area.
Equidistant projections preserve particular distances.
State Plane systems are designed for accurate regional and local mapping in the United States.
UTM divides most of the world into 60 zones, each 6 degrees of longitude wide.
UTM coordinates are measured in meters.
